title: Immediately raise core defence spending to 5% of GDP
headline: The single most expensive thing on this page: £74bn a year.
description: NATO members agreed in June 2025 to spend 5% of GDP on defence and security by 2035, of which 3.5% is core defence and 1.5% is resilience and infrastructure. This recommendation asks for 5% on core defence alone, now. The OBR's forecast already has core defence rising from 2.4% of GDP in 2025-26 to 3.0% by 2030-31 to meet the 3.5%-by-2035 commitment. The cost here is the gap between 5% and that path, multiplied by nominal GDP. It is larger than the entire education budget.

baselinePolicy.text: The OBR assumes defence spending rises from 2.4% of GDP in 2025-26 to 3.0% by 2030-31, on the way to the Government's commitment of 3.5% by 2035.

source.quote: spending on defence rises from 2.4 per cent in 2025-26 to 3.0 per cent by the end of the forecast

alreadyIncludes: Defence RDEL of £42.0bn and CDEL of £31.5bn in 2028-29 (Spending Review 2025, Tables 5.3 and 5.4).

source.table: Paragraph 4.15 and the nominal GDP forecast

rawSource.note: The OBR publishes the two ends of the path, 2.4% in 2025-26 and 3.0% in 2030-31, not the years between. Those are filled in by straight-line interpolation, which is our assumption, not the OBR's. The cost is then (5% − that share) × nominal GDP.

caveats: The share is split 43% capital and 57% day-to-day, the split in the Spending Review's own defence settlement for 2028-29 (£31.5bn capital, £42.0bn resource). Capital spending does not count against the stability rule, so the split matters as much as the total.
Nobody has costed this policy. The arithmetic is ours: a target share of GDP against the forecast share.
Money is not capability. Whether defence could absorb this much this fast is a question about industry and people, not about the public finances.

considerations.text: NATO's 5% is core defence plus 1.5% of GDP on resilience and infrastructure, and the target date is 2035. Applying 5% to core defence alone, immediately, goes well beyond what the alliance agreed.

The OBR already notes that meeting existing commitments leaves unprotected day-to-day spending falling 4.4% a year in real terms at the end of the forecast. An uplift of this size inside a fixed envelope would have to come from somewhere else, or from borrowing.

sources.quote: falling by 4.4 per cent a year in real terms in the final two years of the forecast
